name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
title: Security of Connected Medical Devices
answer: Connected medical devices are instruments that hold a network link, whether that is an infusion pump on a hospital wireless LAN, a pacemaker with a bedside monitor, or a home glucose reader that uploads to a phone. The security question covers the device itself, the apps and servers it talks to, and the clinical workflow that depends on it. It sits inside the wider field of medical device security, alongside software as a medical device and the AI models that increasingly run on or behind these products. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, a reminder that many connected devices now carry a learned component as well as a radio.

sections.body: Connected medical devices are instruments that hold a network link, whether that is an infusion pump on a hospital wireless LAN, a pacemaker with a bedside monitor, or a home glucose reader that uploads to a phone. The security question covers the device itself, the apps and servers it talks to, and the clinical workflow that depends on it. It sits inside the wider field of medical device security, alongside software as a medical device and the AI models that increasingly run on or behind these products. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, a reminder that many connected devices now carry a learned component as well as a radio.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A connected device is usually a small computer with a radio, running a stripped down operating system on limited memory and power. It reaches the network over Wi Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, or a proprietary clinical band, and it often speaks to a vendor cloud before anything reaches the hospital record. Hospitals segment these devices onto separate network zones, use inventory and monitoring tools to see what is attached, and patch through the manufacturer rather than on their own schedule. The weak points tend to be old firmware, shared default passwords, and long support lives that outlast the software inside.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Security work on these devices follows the product lifecycle rather than a single audit. Manufacturers do threat modeling and risk assessment during design, then submit evidence on cybersecurity to regulators as part of premarket review. After release they run a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process, publish advisories, and ship patches, while hospitals maintain an inventory, monitor network traffic for odd behavior, and rehearse what to do if a device must be pulled offline. Testing includes penetration testing, fuzzing of communication protocols, and review of third party components. Because a fix can require a firmware update or even a physical service visit, response is slower than in ordinary IT.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rules come from several directions at once. Regulators in the United States and Europe expect cybersecurity information in device submissions and require manufacturers to manage vulnerabilities after sale, and hospital accreditation and privacy law add duties around patient data. Liability matters too: the site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and device makers face similar exposure when a flaw contributes to harm. Provenance questions follow the software bill of materials, so a hospital can tell which devices contain a given open source library when a flaw is announced. Contracts, warranties, and right to repair terms shape how quickly a buyer can act without the vendor.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward security that is designed in and evidenced continuously rather than checked once. Regulators are moving to formal premarket cybersecurity requirements and to mandatory software bills of materials, which makes the component list of a device a routine procurement document. Hospitals are consolidating device inventories into the same asset systems they use for other IT, and monitoring is shifting from periodic scans to continuous traffic analysis. On the device side, more of the clinical logic is moving into updatable software and hosted models, which shortens patch cycles but widens the attack surface. The open question is support life: a device may stay implanted or installed for a decade while the software inside it ages much faster.
